cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XVIII
The fight with Irus;\nthe warning to Amphinomus; Penelope shines before the suitors.
And there came a public beggar, who used to beg
through the town of Ithaca,\nnotorious for his ravening belly,
eating and drinking without end; no strength was in him
and no force, but in bulk he was very big to look at.
Arnaeus was his name — his honored mother gave it\nhim at birth; but Irus all the young men called him,
because he would run messages whenever anyone bade him.
He came now to drive Odysseus from his own house,\nand abusing him he spoke winged words:
"Off the porch, old man —\nor be dragged off quick by the foot.
Don't you see how they're all winking at me,\ntelling me to drag you? I am ashamed to, even so.
Up, then — before our quarrel comes to fists."
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"Man possessed — I do you no harm, I say you none;\nI grudge no one giving to you, however much he takes up.
This threshold will hold the two of us. You have no need
to grudge what is other men's. You seem to me a wanderer\njust as I am — and prosperity is the gods' to give.
Only do not challenge me too far with\nyour fists, or you will anger me,
and old as I am I will spatter your chest and lips\nwith blood. And I would have the more peace for it
tomorrow: for I do not think you would come back a\nsecond time to the hall of Laertes' son Odysseus."
Then Irus the vagrant answered him in anger:
"Listen to the glutton — how he rattles on,\nlike an old woman at her oven! I'll plan him a nasty turn:
hit him with both hands and knock every tooth from\nhis jaws to the ground, like a crop-raiding sow's.
Belt up now, so all these men may know us as we\nfight. But how would you fight a younger man?"
So, before the high doors, on the polished
threshold, the two of them bristled\nat each other with whole hearts.
And the sacred strength of Antinous took note of them,
and breaking into easy laughter he called to the suitors:
"Friends — nothing like this has ever happened yet:
what sport the god has brought into this house!
The stranger and Irus are wrangling with each other to\nfight it out with fists. Quick — let us match them!"
So he spoke; and they all sprang up laughing\nand crowded round the ill-dressed beggars.
And Antinous spoke among them, Eupeithes' son:
"Hear me, lordly suitors, while I say a word.
There are goats' paunches lying at the fire,\nwhich we set by for supper, filled with fat and blood.
Whichever of the two wins and proves the better man,\nlet him stand up and take his pick of them;
and ever after he shall feast with us,\nand no other beggar will we let inside to beg among us."
So spoke Antinous, and his word pleased them well.
Then Odysseus of the many designs,\nwith craft in mind, spoke among them:
"Friends, there is no way an old man can fight a\nyounger one — a man worn down by misery. But the belly,
that worker of evil, eggs me on,\nto go down under his blows.
Come then, all of you swear me a strong oath:
that no one, doing Irus a favor, will strike me a foul\nblow with a heavy hand, and force me under for him."
So he spoke; and they all swore the oath as he demanded.
And when they had sworn and sealed the oath entire,\nthe sacred strength of Telemachus spoke among them:
"Stranger — if your heart and your proud spirit move\nyou to beat this man off, fear none of the other
Achaeans: whoever strikes you\nwill have more than one to fight.
Your host is myself; and the kings second it,\nAntinous and Eurymachus, sound-thinking men both."
So he spoke, and they all approved. And Odysseus\ngirded his rags about his loins, and bared his thighs —
beautiful, massive — and his broad shoulders came\nto light, his chest, his heavy arms. And Athena
came close and filled out the limbs\nof the shepherd of the people.
And the suitors, every one,\nwere amazed beyond all measure,
and a man would say, with a glance at his neighbor:
"Irus un-Irused soon — a self-invited beating!
Look what a thigh the old man\nshows from under those rags."
So they spoke; and Irus' heart\nwas stirred — for the worse.
Even so the serving-men girded him and led him out by\nforce, in terror, the flesh trembling on his limbs.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Better you were not alive,\nyou ox of a braggart, nor ever born,
if you shiver and fear so terribly before this man —
an old man, worn out with the misery that has found him.
But I will tell you this, and it will be accomplished:
if this man beats you and proves the better man,
I will throw you in a black ship and send you to the\nmainland, to King Echetus, the maimer of all mankind,
who will slice away your nose\nand ears with the pitiless bronze
and tear off your parts and give\nthem raw to the dogs to share."
So he spoke; and a still greater\ntrembling seized Irus' limbs.
But they led him into the middle;\nand both men put up their hands.
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus debated whether to\nhit him so the life would leave him where he fell,
or to hit him gently and just stretch him on the ground.
And as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better way:
to strike gently, so the Achaeans\nwould not take note of him.
Then both put up their guard;\nIrus drove at the right shoulder,
but he struck the neck under\nthe ear, and crushed the bones
inward: at once the red blood came up in his mouth,
and he went down bleating in the dust,\nteeth clenched together,
heels drumming the ground. And the lordly suitors\nthrew up their hands and died laughing. Then Odysseus
took him by the foot and dragged him out through the porch
to the courtyard and the colonnade\ngates; and there he propped him
against the courtyard fence, sitting up,\nand pushed his stick into his hand,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
"Sit there now, and keep off the pigs and dogs,\nand stop lording it over strangers and beggars,
wretch that you are, or a worse evil yet may find you."
He spoke, and slung about his shoulders his beggar's\npouch, full of holes, hanging by a twisted cord,
and went back to the threshold\nand sat down. And they went inside
laughing sweetly, and saluted him with words:
"May Zeus give you, stranger,\nand the other deathless gods,
whatever you most desire, whatever is dear to your heart —\nyou who stopped that insatiable one from begging
through the land! For soon we will haul him to the mainland,\nto King Echetus, the maimer of all mankind."
So they spoke; and noble Odysseus\nrejoiced at the omen of the words.
And Antinous set beside him the great paunch,\nfilled with fat and blood; and Amphinomus
took up two loaves from the basket and set them by him,\nand pledged him with a golden cup, and said:
"Your health, father stranger! May happiness be yours
in time to come — though now you\nare held fast in many evils."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Amphinomus — you seem to me a man of good sense,
and such was the father you come from:\nI have heard his good name —
Nisus of Dulichium, a brave man and a rich one.
They say you are his son; and you seem a civil man.
So I will tell you something. Mark it; hear me out.
The earth breeds nothing feebler than a man —\nof all things that breathe and move on the face of it.
He tells himself he will never\nsuffer evil in time to come,
as long as the gods lend him\nprowess and his knees are quick;
but when the blessed gods bring hard days too to pass,\nthese too he bears — unwilling, on an enduring heart.
For such is the mind of men who live on earth:
it is weather — whatever day the\nfather of gods and men brings on.
I too was once set fair to be fortunate among men,
and I did many reckless things, giving way to my force\nand power, trusting in my father and my brothers.
So let no man ever be lawless in anything,\nbut keep in silence whatever gifts the gods may give.
Such recklessness I see the suitors devising here —\nshearing away the goods, dishonoring the wife
of a man who, I tell you, will not long be far
from his friends and his fathers' land.\nHe is very close. But you —
may your own fate steal you home\ninstead; may you not meet him
the day he comes back to his own dear country.
For not without blood, I think, will they be parted,
the suitors and that man,\nonce he comes in under his roof."
So he spoke, and poured, and drank the honey-sweet wine,
then gave the cup back into the\nhands of the marshal of the people.
And that man went off down the hall with an aching heart,
head sinking down: for his spirit foresaw the evil.
But even so he did not escape\nhis fate: Athena bound him too,
to be broken under the hands and spear of Telemachus.
Back he went, and sat down on the\nchair from which he had risen.
And now the goddess, gray-eyed Athena, put it in the\nmind of Icarius' daughter, watchful-minded Penelope,
to show herself to the suitors: so she might open
their hearts wide as sails,\nand come to stand more precious
in her husband's eyes, and her son's,\nthan she had been before.
She laughed — an empty laugh —\nand spoke a word, and named her:
"Eurynome, my heart longs — as it never has before —\nto show myself to the suitors, hateful as they are.
And I would say a word to my son — the better for him:
not to keep such company with the overweening suitors,\nwho speak him fair and mean him evil behind."
And Eurynome the housekeeper answered her:
"Yes, child — all this you have said as it should be.
Go then, and speak your word to your son; hide nothing.
But first wash your skin, and put a shine on your cheeks:
do not go with your face all stained like this with tears.\nGrief without respite makes everything worse.
And your son is now the age you prayed the deathless\nones so long to let you see: a bearded man."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her:
"Eurynome, do not coax me so — out of love,\nI know — to wash my skin and put a gloss upon it.
Whatever bloom I had, the gods who hold Olympus destroyed\nit the day that man went off in the hollow ships.
But tell Autonoe and Hippodamia to\ncome and stand beside me in the hall:
alone I will not go among men. I would be ashamed."
So she spoke; and the old woman went off through the\nhall to carry word to the women and hurry them along.
Then the goddess, gray-eyed Athena,\nthought of one thing more:
over Icarius' daughter she poured sweet sleep,\nand she slept, leaning back, and all her joints went loose
right there on the couch.\nAnd meanwhile the shining goddess
was giving her immortal gifts, to make the Achaeans stare.
she cleansed her lovely face with the\nambrosial balm that crowned Cytherea
anoints herself with, when she\ngoes to the Graces' lovely dance;
and she made her taller and fuller to the eye,\nand made her whiter than sawn ivory.
That done, the shining goddess went away,\nand the white-armed handmaids came in from the hall,
talking as they came; and the sweet sleep let her go.
She rubbed her cheeks with her hands and said:
"Soft — the softest of trances\nwrapped me round, for all my anguish.
If only pure Artemis would give me a death as soft,
this very instant — so that I\nneed no longer mourn at heart,
wasting my life away, longing for my dear husband
and his every excellence:\nfor he stood out among the Achaeans."
So speaking she came down from her shining upper room —\nnot alone: two handmaids followed with her.
And when she reached the suitors, shining among women,\nshe stood beside the pillar of the close-built roof,
holding her glistening veil before her cheeks,\na trusted handmaid standing on either side.
And their knees went slack on the spot,\ntheir hearts spellbound with desire,
and every man prayed to lie in bed beside her.
But she spoke to Telemachus, her dear son:
"Telemachus, your mind is no\nlonger steady, nor your thought.
While you were still a boy,\nyou turned shrewder plans than this;
but now that you are grown,\ncome to the measure of manhood,
so that a stranger, looking at your height and beauty,\nwould say you must be some rich man's son —
your mind and thought are no longer as they should be.
What a thing has been done here in the halls:
you let the stranger be manhandled so!
What now — if a stranger, sitting in our house,\nshould come to harm from such ugly hauling-about?
On you the shame and the disgrace\nwould fall, among all men."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mother mine, I cannot resent your anger at this.
But I do take note in my heart, I do know each thing,
the good and the worse alike. Before, I was still a child.
Yet I cannot manage to think out everything wisely:
these men unhinge me — crowding me this side and that,\nplotting their mischief; and I have no helpers.
Still, the bout of the stranger and Irus did not go as\nthe suitors intended: the stranger was the stronger.
If only — father Zeus, Athena, Apollo! —\nthe suitors in our house would nod their heads
like that, beaten and broken, some in the courtyard,
some inside the house, and the limbs of each gone slack,\nthe way that Irus over there at the courtyard gates
sits lolling his head like a man dead drunk,\nand cannot stand upright on his feet, or go
home, wherever home is — since his own limbs are slack."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And Eurymachus addressed Penelope with words:
"Daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope,\nif all the Achaeans through Iasian Argos could see you,
more suitors yet would be feasting in your house\nfrom tomorrow morning: for you surpass all women
in form and stature, and in the balanced mind within."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Eurymachus, my excellence — my face, my figure —\nthe deathless ones destroyed the day the Argives
boarded ship for Ilium, and my husband Odysseus with them.
If he came back — if he watched over this life of\nmine — my fame would be greater so, and lovelier.
Now I only grieve: so many evils the god has driven at me.
Truly, when he went, leaving his fathers' land,\nhe took me by the right hand at the wrist and said:
'Wife — I do not think the strong-greaved Achaeans\nwill all come home from Troy unharmed and whole:
the Trojans too, they say, are men of war,\nspear-throwers, drawers of the bow,
mounters of swift-footed horses — such as\ndecide soonest the great strife of leveling war.
So I cannot know whether the god will bring me back,
or I go down there in Troy.\nLet everything here be your care.
Remember my father and my mother in these halls\nas now, or even more, while I am far away.
But when you see our son a bearded man,\nmarry whom you will, and leave your house behind.'
So he spoke it, that man.\nAnd now it is all being accomplished:
the night will come when the\nmarriage I loathe will meet me —
my cursed self, whose happiness Zeus has torn away.
But this bitter shame comes over my heart and spirit:
this is not what suitors' custom used to be.
Men who would woo a good woman, a rich man's daughter,\nand contend with one another for her —
they drive up cattle of their own, and fat sheep,
a feast for the bride's people,\nand they give her shining gifts.
They do not devour another man's living, scot-free."
So she spoke; and much-enduring noble Odysseus was glad
that she drew gifts out of them, charming their hearts
with honeyed words, while her\nmind was bent on other things.
Then Antinous answered her, Eupeithes' son:
"Daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope,\nthe gifts — whatever any Achaean wishes to bring here,
accept them: it is not good manners to refuse a gift.
But we are not going to our lands, nor anywhere else,\nuntil you marry whichever of the Achaeans is best."
So spoke Antinous, and his word pleased them well,\nand each man sent a herald off to bring his gifts.
For Antinous he brought a great embroidered robe,\nbeautiful, and in it were brooches, twelve in all,
of gold, fitted with well-bent clasps.
For Eurymachus one brought a necklace, richly worked
in gold, strung with pieces of amber, bright as the sun.
For Eurydamas two henchmen brought a pair of earrings,
triple-dropped like mulberries;\nand much grace glinted from them.
And out of the house of lord Peisander, Polyctor's son,
a henchman brought a neck-band, a jewel of great beauty.
And so one Achaean after another brought his lovely gift.
Then she went up to her upper room, shining among women,
and her handmaids carried the beautiful gifts beside her.
But the men turned to the dance and to lovely song
and took their pleasure there,\nand waited for evening to come.
And as they took their pleasure,\nthe black evening came upon them.
At once they set up three braziers in the halls to\ngive them light, and heaped dry kindling round —
long-seasoned, bone-dry, new-split with the bronze —
and mixed in pine-brands. And turn by turn the slave-women
of enduring-hearted Odysseus\nkept the flame alive. And to them
he himself spoke, Zeus-born Odysseus of the many designs:
"Slave-women of Odysseus, of your master so long gone:
go through to the rooms where the honored queen is;\nturn the spindle at her side, and cheer her heart,
sitting there in her chamber,\nor card the wool with your hands.
I will keep up the light for all these men myself.
Even if they choose to wait for fair-throned Dawn,\nthey will not outlast me. I am a very patient man."
So he spoke; and they burst out\nlaughing, glancing at one another.
And fair-cheeked Melantho jeered at him shamefully —\nDolius fathered her, but Penelope brought her up
and cherished her like her own child,\nand gave her toys to her heart's desire;
yet even so no grief for Penelope touched her mind,\nbut she slept with Eurymachus, and loved him.
She now jeered at Odysseus with words of abuse:
"You sorry stranger — you must be some kind of half-wit:
you will not go and sleep at the smithy's house,
or some public shed — no,\nyou stand here running your mouth,
bold as brass among all these men, and your heart feels
no fear. Either the wine has\nhold of your wits, or your mind
is always of this sort — that is why you babble so idly.
Or are you giddy because you beat that vagrant Irus?
Watch out that no better man than Irus stands up soon,
who will box both sides of your skull with his heavy hands
and send you out of the house all fouled with blood."
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"One word to Telemachus, you bitch,\nand I go straight to him now,
for what you are saying — and he will\ncut you limb from limb on the spot."
So speaking, he set the women scattering in terror:
off they went through the house,\nand the knees of every one
went slack with fear; they thought he spoke the truth.
But he took his stand by the burning braziers, tending
the light, and watched them all;\nand other things his heart
was pondering deep within —\nthings not destined to fall short.
And Athena would not let the lordly suitors hold back\nfrom heart-stinging outrage — so that pain might sink
still deeper into Laertes' son Odysseus.
So Eurymachus, Polybus' son, began to speak among them,
baiting Odysseus; and he raised\na laugh among his companions:
"Hear me, you suitors of the far-famed queen,\nwhile I say what the heart in my breast commands.
Not without god's guidance has\nthis man come to Odysseus' house —
at any rate the blaze of the torches seems to me to come
straight off his head: for there\nis not one hair on it, not a wisp."
He spoke, and turned to Odysseus, sacker of cities:
"Stranger — would you take a hire, if I took you on,
out at the end of my lands — your pay will not fail you —\npicking stones for walls and planting tall trees?
There I would furnish you bread the year round,
and put clothes on your body,\nand give you sandals for your feet.
But no: you have learned bad ways, and you will not
set yourself to work; you would\nrather cringe through the town
begging, to feed that bottomless belly of yours."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Eurymachus — if only the two of\nus could have a match at work,
in the spring season, when the days grow long:
at mowing — I with a well-curved scythe in hand,\nand you with one like it — a trial of work,
fasting right up to dark,\nand the grass still standing thick.
Or oxen to drive — the very best oxen,\ntawny and big, both of them fat with grass,
matched in age and pull, their strength no trifle,\nand a four-acre field, the soil giving under the plow:
then you would see whether I could\ncut a furrow straight and long.
Or if the son of Cronos stirred up war — from anywhere —\nthis very day, and I had a shield and two spears
and a helmet all of bronze, fitted to my temples:
then you would see me mixed into the front fighters,
and you would not talk and talk,\njeering at this belly of mine.
But no — you are full of insolence, and your mind is hard,
and no doubt you fancy yourself a big man and a mighty,
because you keep company with few — and none of them good.
But if Odysseus came — if he reached his own country —\nthose doors, wide as they are, would all at once
be too narrow for you,\nflying through the porch for the street."
So he spoke; and Eurymachus grew the angrier at heart,
and glaring from under his brows he spoke winged words:
"Wretch — I will finish you off\nfor good, for the way you talk,
bold as brass among all these men, and your heart feels
no fear. Either the wine has\nhold of your wits, or your mind
is always of this sort — that is why you babble so idly.
Or are you giddy because you beat that vagrant Irus?"
With that he seized a footstool. But Odysseus\nsank down at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium,
in fear of Eurymachus; and the stool struck the cupbearer
on the right hand: his wine-jug\nrang on the floor where it fell,
and the man groaned and went over backward in the dust.
And the suitors raised a din through the shadowy halls,\nand a man would say, with a glance at his neighbor:
"If only the stranger had died\non his wanderings somewhere else
before he ever came! He would\nnot have brought all this uproar.
Now here we are brawling over\nbeggars; there will be no joy
even in the good feast, now the worse is winning out."
And the sacred strength of Telemachus spoke among them:
"You are possessed — you have\ngone mad. You can no longer hide
what you have eaten and drunk. Some god is goading you on.
No — you have feasted well: now go home and lie down,
whenever the spirit moves you.\nNot that I am driving anyone out."
So he spoke; and they all bit their lips and stared\nin wonder at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
Then Amphinomus rose and spoke among them —\nthe shining son of Nisus, of the lord Aretias' line:
"Friends — no man should take offense at a just word\nspoken, and answer it with wrangling and hard speech.
Do not knock the stranger about, nor any other\nof the slaves in the house of godlike Odysseus.
Come — let the cupbearer pour first-drops in the cups,\nso we can make libation and go home to bed;
and the stranger — let us leave\nhim in the halls of Odysseus
for Telemachus to see to:\nit is his dear house the man has come to."
So he spoke, and the word he spoke pleased all of them.
And the hero Moulius mixed the bowl for them,\nthe herald from Dulichium, Amphinomus' henchman;
he served it round to all in turn; and they poured\nto the blessed gods, and drank the honey-sweet wine.
And when they had poured, and drunk\nas much as their hearts would have,
they went their ways to bed, each man to his own house.
